overview.text: A determinant is a single number assigned to a square matrix; for a 2 × 2 matrix with rows (a, b) and (c, d), it is ad − bc. It summarizes how the matrix’s linear transformation changes space: in two dimensions, its absolute value gives the area scale factor, and in any dimension its absolute value gives the volume scale factor. The sign records orientation. A zero determinant means the transformation collapses space and the matrix is not invertible; a nonzero determinant means it is invertible. This makes determinants useful for analyzing square systems of linear equations: when the coefficient matrix has a nonzero determinant, Cramer’s rule can find the system’s unique solution.

key_facts.text: For a 2 × 2 matrix [[a, b], [c, d]], the determinant is ad − bc. It can be written det(A) or with vertical bars around the matrix.
A square matrix is invertible exactly when its determinant is nonzero; a zero determinant signals that it has no inverse.
In two dimensions, the absolute value of a determinant is the factor by which a matrix transformation scales area; in higher dimensions it gives the volume scale factor.
The determinant’s sign can distinguish orientation: for example, swapping two coordinates reflects the plane and gives determinant −1.
Cramer’s rule uses determinants to solve a square system of linear equations when its coefficient matrix has a nonzero determinant.
